newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia to ease media ownership limits - papers.
newsitem.headline: Australia to ease media ownership limits - papers.

text.p: Australia planned to ease tough media ownership limits in a move that could allow media tycoons Kerry Packer and Rupert Murdoch to expand their empires and foreigners to take bigger media stakes, newspapers said on Thursday.

The plan would allow a single proprietor to own one newspaper and one television station in the major cities of Sydney and Melbourne and would raise foreign ownership limits to 25 percent from 15 percent.
The plan has been drawn up as a compromise to allow the government to ease media limits while satisfying government parliamentarians' concerns over diversity, newspapers reported.
Cabinet may consider the compromise deal within weeks.

The plan would clear the way for Packer, Australia's richest man, to take over newspaper group John Fairfax Holdings Ltd and for Murdoch's News Corp to increase its shareholding in the Seven Network Ltd.
The government is reviewing rules set by the former Labor government limiting cross-ownership in newspapers and television stations in major markets to 15 percent.
Capital cities with one major daily newspaper -- Brisbane, Perth, Adelaide and Hobart -- would be exempt from the changes, The Australian Financial Review reported.
Under the changes, Packer's Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd would have to sell the Review if he took over Fairfax.

Murdoch's position was unclear. Although News Ltd owns tabloids in Sydney and Melbourne as well as the national daily The Australian, the Review quoted coalition sources as saying the government was considering a "grandfather" clause that would allow News to keep all its papers. Government officials were not immediately available to comment on the reports.
The Labor opposition rejected the reported reforms.
"It's a very silly idea. We need more media diversity in Australia, not less," opposition deputy leader Gareth Evans told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.
Evans said the government was trying to secure the backing of major media proprietors.
"There's no reason to suppose this is anything other than an attempt by the government to scramble for some kind of preferment from one of the major proprietors," he said.
"There's no other ground of principle that could possibly lie behind this."
The changes would need approval by parliament's upper house, the Senate, where the government does not have a majority.
Foreigners are currently limited to owning 15 percent of television stations and 25 percent of newspapers.
The Sydney Morning Herald and The Australian suggested a general 25 percent limit could be set, but the Review said an industry-wide 35 percent limit could be imposed.
